title: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition
tldr: Residual networks (ResNets) reformulate layers to learn residual functions, enabling training of networks up to 152 layers deep with improved accuracy and without degradation, winning ILSVRC & COCO 2015 across classification, detection, and segmentation.
abstract: Deeper neural networks are harder to train due to degradation: accuracy saturates then drops as depth increases, even with normalized initialization and batch normalization. We introduce a residual learning framework where layers learn residual functions with reference to their inputs, implemented via identity shortcut connections. This eases optimization, allowing networks up to 152 layers deep to train effectively. On ImageNet, a 152-layer ResNet achieves 3.57% top-5 error (ensemble), winning ILSVRC 2015 classification. The same principle yields 28% relative improvement on COCO object detection and wins first place in ILSVRC & COCO 2015 across detection, localization, and segmentation tasks.

blocks.text: Deep convolutional networks have driven breakthroughs in image classification by stacking layers to integrate low-, mid-, and high-level features. Evidence shows depth is critical: leading ImageNet results use 16–30 layers. Yet deeper networks face a degradation problem: accuracy saturates then degrades rapidly, even on training data. This is not overfitting—adding layers to a deep model increases training error.

The degradation problem implies an optimization difficulty: if a deeper model can be constructed by adding identity-mapping layers to a shallower one, the deeper model should have no higher training error. But solvers fail to find such solutions in feasible time.

We address this by reformulating layers to learn residual functions: instead of fitting H(x), we fit F(x) = H(x) − x, so H(x) = F(x) + x. This is implemented via shortcut connections that add the input x to the output of stacked layers. Identity shortcuts add no parameters or computation, and the network trains end-to-end with SGD.

blocks.title: The Degradation Problem
blocks.text: Deeper plain networks have higher training error than shallower ones, even when the shallower network’s solution space is a subset of the deeper one. This reveals an optimization difficulty, not a capacity issue.

Residual representations appear in VLAD and Fisher Vectors for image retrieval, and in multigrid methods for solving PDEs, where residual solutions between scales simplify optimization. Shortcut connections have been explored in MLPs, auxiliary classifiers, and highway networks.

Highway networks use gated shortcuts with parameters, allowing layers to learn non-residual functions when gates close. In contrast, ResNets always learn residual functions via parameter-free identity shortcuts, ensuring information always passes through.

blocks.title: Key Difference from Highway Networks
blocks.text: ResNets use identity shortcuts (no parameters, never closed), while highway networks use gated shortcuts (parameters, can close). ResNets consistently learn residual functions; highway networks do not demonstrate gains with >100 layers.
3.1 Residual Learning

Let H(x) be the desired mapping for a stack of layers. Instead of learning H(x) directly, we learn the residual F(x) = H(x) − x, so H(x) = F(x) + x. If identity mapping is optimal, it is easier to push F(x) toward zero than to fit H(x) = x with stacked nonlinear layers.
Empirically, residual functions in trained ResNets have small responses (Fig. 7), suggesting identity mappings provide good preconditioning for optimization.
3.2 Identity Mapping by Shortcuts

A residual block is defined as y = F(x, {W_i}) + x, where F is the residual function (e.g., two 3×3 conv layers with ReLU). Shortcut connections add x to F(x) via element-wise addition. If dimensions change, we use a projection shortcut: y = F(x, {W_i}) + W_s x, where W_s is a 1×1 conv layer.

blocks.caption: Residual learning building block: a stack of layers (e.g., two 3×3 convs) learns F(x), and the shortcut adds x to F(x).
blocks.label: Figure 2

blocks.title: Shortcut Connections
blocks.text: Shortcut connections skip one or more layers, adding the input directly to the output. In ResNets, they are identity mappings (or projections when dimensions change) and add no extra parameters or computation.
points: Identity shortcuts: y = F(x) + x (same dimensions).
Projection shortcuts: y = F(x) + W_s x (dimensions change).
No extra parameters or FLOPs for identity shortcuts.

blocks.text: 3.3 Network Architectures

We design plain and residual networks for ImageNet, inspired by VGG nets but with fewer filters and lower complexity. Plain networks use 3×3 conv layers with two rules: (1) same number of filters for the same output size, (2) double filters when halving feature map size. Residual networks insert shortcuts into plain networks.

blocks.caption: Example architectures for ImageNet. Left: VGG-19 (19.6B FLOPs). Middle: 34-layer plain network (3.6B FLOPs). Right: 34-layer residual network (3.6B FLOPs). Dotted shortcuts handle dimension changes.
blocks.label: Figure 3

blocks.text: For deeper networks, we use a bottleneck design: each residual block has three layers (1×1, 3×3, 1×1 convs), where 1×1 layers reduce and restore dimensions, leaving the 3×3 layer as a bottleneck. This reduces parameters and FLOPs while maintaining accuracy.

blocks.caption: Bottleneck residual block for ResNet-50/101/152. Left: 2-layer block (ResNet-34). Right: 3-layer bottleneck block.
blocks.label: Figure 5

blocks.text: 3.4 Implementation

We train on ImageNet with scale augmentation (shorter side in [256, 480]), random 224×224 crops, horizontal flips, and per-pixel mean subtraction. We use batch normalization after each conv layer, He initialization, SGD with momentum 0.9, weight decay 0.0001, and a mini-batch size of 256. Learning rate starts at 0.1 and is divided by 10 when error plateaus. No dropout is used.
For testing, we use 10-crop testing for comparisons and fully-convolutional multi-scale testing for best results (shorter side in {224, 256, 384, 480, 640}).
4.1 ImageNet Classification

On ImageNet 2012 (1.28M training, 50K validation, 1000 classes), we evaluate plain and residual networks. Plain networks (18/34 layers) show degradation: the 34-layer net has higher training and validation error than the 18-layer net (Table 2, Fig. 4 left).

blocks.caption: Training on ImageNet. Thin curves: training error. Bold curves: validation error (center crop). Left: plain networks (18/34 layers). Right: ResNets (18/34 layers). ResNets avoid degradation and benefit from increased depth.
blocks.label: Figure 4

blocks.text: ResNets (18/34 layers) reverse this: the 34-layer ResNet has lower training error and better validation accuracy than the 18-layer ResNet (Table 2, Fig. 4 right). Identity shortcuts (option A) work well; projection shortcuts (option B) are slightly better (Table 3).

Bottleneck ResNets (50/101/152 layers) use 3-layer blocks (1×1, 3×3, 1×1 convs) to reduce parameters. The 152-layer ResNet has 11.3B FLOPs, less than VGG-16 (15.3B). Single-model results: ResNet-152 achieves 4.49% top-5 error on validation (Table 4). An ensemble of 6 models achieves 3.57% top-5 error on the test set (Table 5), winning ILSVRC 2015 classification.
4.2 CIFAR-10 and Analysis

On CIFAR-10 (50K training, 10K test, 10 classes), we use simple architectures: 6n + 2 layers (n = 3, 5, 7, 9 → 20, 32, 44, 56 layers). Plain networks suffer from degradation (Fig. 6 left), while ResNets benefit from increased depth (Fig. 6 middle).

blocks.caption: Training on CIFAR-10. Dashed lines: training error. Bold lines: testing error. Left: plain networks. Middle: ResNets. Right: ResNets with 110 and 1202 layers.
blocks.label: Figure 6

blocks.text: A 110-layer ResNet achieves 6.43% test error (Table 6), among the best results. A 1202-layer ResNet trains successfully (training error <0.1%) but overfits (7.93% test error). Stronger regularization (e.g., dropout) may help.

Analysis of layer responses (Fig. 7) shows ResNets have smaller response magnitudes than plain nets, supporting the hypothesis that residual functions are closer to zero. Deeper ResNets have even smaller responses per layer.

blocks.caption: Standard deviations of layer responses on CIFAR-10. Top: layers in original order. Bottom: responses ranked in descending order. ResNets have smaller responses than plain nets.
blocks.label: Figure 7

blocks.text: 4.3 Object Detection on PASCAL and COCO

ResNets generalize to object detection. Using Faster R-CNN, ResNet-101 improves mAP by 3.2% on PASCAL VOC 2007 (73.2% → 76.4%) and by 6.0% on COCO (mAP@[.5,.95]: 21.2% → 27.2%), a 28% relative improvement (Tables 7, 8).

With improvements (box refinement, global context, multi-scale testing), ResNet-101 achieves 85.6% mAP on VOC 2007 and 83.8% on VOC 2012 (Tables 10, 11), and 55.7% mAP@.5 / 34.9% mAP@[.5,.95] on COCO test-dev (Table 9). An ensemble wins COCO 2015 detection (59.0% mAP@.5, 37.4% mAP@[.5,.95]).

On ImageNet detection, ResNet-101 achieves 58.8% mAP (single model) and 62.1% mAP (ensemble), winning ILSVRC 2015 (Table 12). On ImageNet localization, ResNet-101 reduces top-5 error to 8.9% (ensemble), a 64% relative improvement over ILSVRC 2014 (Table 14).

Deeper networks should theoretically perform no worse than shallower ones, as the added layers can learn identity mappings. Yet in practice, with the network depth increasing, accuracy gets saturated and then degrades rapidly. This degradation is not caused by overfitting, and adding more layers to a suitably deep model leads to higher training error (Fig. 1).

blocks.caption: Training error (left) and test error (right) on CIFAR-10 with 20-layer and 56-layer plain networks. The deeper network has higher training error.
blocks.label: Figure 1

blocks.title: Key Insight
blocks.text: The solver struggles to approximate identity mappings with multiple nonlinear layers, even though such mappings should be trivial.

Instead of learning an unreferenced mapping H(x), we reformulate the problem as learning a residual function F(x) = H(x) − x. The original mapping becomes F(x) + x. «We hypothesize that it is easier to optimize the residual mapping than to optimize the original, unreferenced mapping.»

blocks.title: Shortcut Connections
blocks.text: The residual function F(x) is implemented via shortcut connections that skip one or more layers. The output y is computed as y = F(x, {W_i}) + x, where F is typically a stack of 2–3 convolutional layers (Fig. 2).
points: Shortcut connections perform identity mapping (or projection if dimensions change).
They add no extra parameters or computational complexity.
The entire network is trained end-to-end with SGD and backpropagation.

blocks.caption: Residual learning building block: a stack of layers learns F(x), and the shortcut adds x to the output.
blocks.label: Figure 2

blocks.text: To the extreme, if an identity mapping were optimal, it would be easier to push the residual to zero than to fit an identity mapping by a stack of nonlinear layers.
ResNets are built by stacking residual blocks. For ImageNet, we use two variants:

blocks.title: Plain Baseline
blocks.text: Inspired by VGG nets, the plain network uses 3×3 convolutional layers with two design rules: (i) same number of filters for the same output feature map size, and (ii) double filters when the feature map size is halved. Downsampling is done via stride-2 convolutions. The network ends with global average pooling and a 1000-way fully-connected layer.
points: 34-layer plain baseline has 3.6 billion FLOPs (18% of VGG-19).
No shortcut connections; layers are stacked directly.

blocks.title: Residual Network
blocks.text: Shortcut connections are added to the plain network to form a residual network. For matching dimensions, identity shortcuts are used (solid lines in Fig. 3). For increasing dimensions, two options exist: (A) zero-padding for identity mapping, or (B) 1×1 convolutional projection.
points: Option A (zero-padding) and B (projection) both outperform plain networks.
Projection shortcuts are only used when dimensions increase; otherwise, identity shortcuts suffice.
Bottleneck design: 1×1, 3×3, 1×1 convolutions reduce and restore dimensions, with the 3×3 layer as the bottleneck.

blocks.caption: Example architectures for ImageNet: VGG-19 (left), plain 34-layer (middle), and residual 34-layer (right). Dotted shortcuts increase dimensions.
blocks.label: Figure 3

blocks.caption: Bottleneck residual block for ResNet-50/101/152: 1×1, 3×3, 1×1 convolutions with identity shortcuts.
blocks.label: Figure 5

blocks.text: The 152-layer ResNet is the deepest network ever presented on ImageNet, while still having lower complexity than VGG nets [41].
ImageNet Classification
On ImageNet, ResNets outperform plain networks and prior state-of-the-art. Our ensemble has 3.57% error on the ImageNet test set, and won the 1st place on the ILSVRC 2015 classification task.

blocks.caption: Training curves on ImageNet: plain networks (left) degrade with depth, while ResNets (right) improve.
blocks.label: Figure 4

blocks.text: CIFAR-10
On CIFAR-10, ResNets with up to 1202 layers are trained successfully. The 110-layer ResNet achieves 6.43% test error, and the 1202-layer network achieves 7.93% test error (Table 6).

blocks.caption: Training on CIFAR-10: plain networks (left) degrade, while ResNets (middle) improve with depth. Right: ResNets with 110 and 1202 layers.
blocks.label: Figure 6

blocks.text: Object Detection and Localization

ResNets generalize to other tasks. «Solely due to our extremely deep representations, we obtain a 28% relative improvement on the COCO object detection dataset.» We won the 1st places on ImageNet detection, ImageNet localization, COCO detection, and COCO segmentation in ILSVRC & COCO 2015 competitions.

Residual learning addresses the degradation problem by making identity mappings easier to learn. The learned residual functions in general have small responses, suggesting that identity mappings provide reasonable preconditioning (Fig. 7).

blocks.caption: Standard deviations of layer responses on CIFAR-10. ResNets have smaller responses than plain networks, indicating residual functions are closer to zero.
blocks.label: Figure 7

blocks.title: Preconditioning
blocks.text: Residual learning reformulates the problem so that the solver can start from an identity mapping and learn small perturbations, rather than learning a new function from scratch.

«If the optimal function is closer to an identity mapping than to a zero mapping, it should be easier for the solver to find the perturbations with reference to an identity mapping, than to learn the function as a new one.»

Training follows standard practices for ImageNet: scale augmentation (shorter side in [256, 480]), random crops, horizontal flips, and per-pixel mean subtraction. Batch normalization (BN) is used after each convolution and before activation. Weights are initialized as in (He et al., 2015), and networks are trained from scratch with SGD (mini-batch size 256, momentum 0.9, weight decay 0.0001). Learning rate starts at 0.1 and is divided by 10 when error plateaus.
For testing, we adopt the fully-convolutional form, and average the scores at multiple scales (images are resized such that the shorter side is in {224, 256, 384, 480, 640}).

Deeper networks degrade: training error rises when adding layers to a sufficiently deep plain network, even though a shallower model’s solution (identity mappings for added layers) should exist. This degradation is not overfitting—it persists on training data.

Normalized initialization (He et al., 2015; Glorot and Bengio, 2010) and batch normalization (Ioffe and Szegedy, 2015) mitigated vanishing/exploding gradients, enabling convergence for tens of layers. Shortcut connections existed (e.g., highway networks (Srivastava et al., 2015)), but used gated, parameterized paths. Multigrid methods (Briggs et al., 2000) in PDEs showed residual reformulations speed convergence.
Replace stacked layers learning H(x) with layers learning F(x) = H(x) – x, so H(x) = F(x) + x. Shortcut connections add x to F(x) via identity mapping (or projection Ws x if dimensions differ).

blocks.title: Residual block
blocks.text: A block computes F(x) via one or more layers (e.g., two 3×3 convs with ReLU), then adds the input x to F(x) element-wise. The shortcut is identity if input/output dimensions match; otherwise, a 1×1 conv (Ws) projects x to match dimensions.
points: No extra parameters for identity shortcuts; projection adds only Ws.
Training remains end-to-end SGD with backpropagation.

blocks.caption: Residual block: input x passes through F(x) and is added to the output via a shortcut.
blocks.label: Figure 1

blocks.title: Why it works
blocks.text: Identity mappings are easier to approximate as residuals (F(x) ≈ 0) than as direct functions (H(x) ≈ x).

items.label: Top-1 error on ImageNet val (ResNet-152, single model)
Relative improvement on COCO detection mAP

blocks.text: ResNets up to 152 layers outperform shallower plain nets and prior state-of-the-art on ImageNet, CIFAR-10, and COCO. Deeper ResNets (50/101/152) consistently improve accuracy without degradation.

Downsides: Over-parameterization in extremely deep thin networks (e.g., ResNet-1202 on CIFAR-10) can overfit without strong regularization. Open question: Optimal depth/width trade-offs for small datasets.

Worth pursuing: Residual learning is a general, simple, and effective principle for training very deep networks. It solves the degradation problem, enables 100+ layer models, and generalizes across tasks (classification, detection, segmentation).
Residual networks are foundations of our submissions to ILSVRC & COCO 2015 competitions, where we won the 1st places on ImageNet detection, localization, COCO detection, and COCO segmentation.

readerIssue.title: Degradation problem in deep networks
readerIssue.text: Readers will struggle with why deeper plain networks (e.g., 34-layer) have higher training error than shallower ones (e.g., 18-layer), despite the deeper network containing the shallower one as a subspace. The plain explanation: the optimization landscape for deep networks is poorly conditioned, making it hard for solvers to find solutions where added layers act as identity mappings. Residual learning reformulates the problem to learn residual functions (H(x) - x) instead of H(x), making identity mappings easier to approximate (by driving weights to zero).

importance.verdict: Introduced residual connections, enabling training of networks with 100+ layers and setting a new paradigm for deep learning architectures.

mustRead.title: Section 3.1: Residual Learning
mustRead.why: Core insight: reformulating layers to learn residual functions (F(x) = H(x) - x) instead of H(x) directly, with the hypothesis that this is easier to optimize.
mustRead.excerpt: Let us consider H(x) as an underlying mapping to be fit by a few stacked layers (not necessarily the entire net), with x denoting the inputs to the first of these layers. If one hypothesizes that multiple nonlinear layers can asymptotically approximate complicated functions, then it is equivalent to hypothesize that they can asymptotically approximate the residual functions, i.e., H(x) − x (assuming that the input and output are of the same dimensions). So rather than expect stacked layers to approximate H(x), we explicitly let these layers approximate a residual function F(x) := H(x) − x. The original function thus becomes F(x) + x.

mustRead.title: Section 3.2: Identity Mapping by Shortcuts
mustRead.why: Mechanism: how residual learning is implemented via shortcut connections, with identity mappings as the default.
mustRead.excerpt: We adopt residual learning to every few stacked layers. A building block is shown in Fig. 2. Formally, in this paper we consider a building block defined as: y = F(x, {W_i}) + x. Here x and y are the input and output vectors of the layers considered. The function F(x, {W_i}) represents the residual mapping to be learned. The operation F + x is performed by a shortcut connection and element-wise addition.

mustRead.title: Section 4.1: ImageNet Classification Results
mustRead.why: Empirical proof: residual networks overcome the degradation problem and achieve state-of-the-art accuracy with extreme depth.
mustRead.excerpt: The 34-layer plain net has higher training error throughout the whole training procedure, even though the solution space of the 18-layer plain network is a subspace of that of the 34-layer one. We have three major observations from Table 2 and Fig. 4. First, the situation is reversed with residual learning – the 34-layer ResNet is better than the 18-layer ResNet (by 2.8%). More importantly, the 34-layer ResNet exhibits considerably lower training error and is generalizable to the validation data.

mustRead.title: Section 4.2: CIFAR-10 Analysis
mustRead.why: Generalization: residual learning works across datasets, enabling training of networks with 1000+ layers.
mustRead.excerpt: We further explore n = 18 that leads to a 110-layer ResNet. In this case, we find that the initial learning rate of 0.1 is slightly too large to start converging. So we use 0.01 to warm up the training until the training error is below 80% (about 400 iterations), and then go back to 0.1 and continue training. This 110-layer network converges well. We also explore an aggressively deep model of over 1000 layers. We set n = 200 that leads to a 1202-layer network, which is trained as described above. Our method shows no optimization difficulty, and this 10^3-layer network is able to achieve training error <0.1%.
